title: Records of mandatory and company drills
plain: Do you know the emergency plans, and can you show records that every required drill was done and written up?
why: Drills only protect the ship if they are planned, done on time and recorded so lessons are not lost.
checks: The company procedure for drills: when to do them, how to record them, what to do if late
The ship's set of emergency plans for each likely emergency
The drill schedule and tracker showing what is done and what is due
Drill records filled in the same way every time
ready: Drill schedule or tracker, up to date
Completed drill records with scenario, summary, lessons and training needs
Risk assessments or permits attached to drill records where used
Emails to the company for any drill that was delayed
Emergency plans in one clear system, easy to find
traps: No company procedure for drills, recording or tracking
Drill record missing scenario, equipment used, lessons or improvement points
Schedule does not match ISM, SOLAS, MARPOL, IGC, IGF or ISPS requirements
Drills overdue for completion
Officer cannot explain the plans or the drill procedure
say: Our SMS tells us which drills are required and how often. We track them on the drill schedule and record each one in the same format, including lessons learnt. If a drill cannot be done on time, such as in bad weather, we tell the company and keep the reply.

practice.q: How do you know no drill is overdue?
a: We use the drill schedule or tracker
Reviewed regularly by the Master and officers
Overdue drills are reported to the company with the reason

practice.q: What do you write in a drill record?
a: Summary, equipment used and safety points
Any improvements for the plan, sent to the company

practice.q: A drill was postponed for bad weather. What did you do?
a: Kept their acknowledgement with the records

tip: Keep one folder, paper or electronic, with the schedule on top and each drill record behind it, so you can find anything in seconds.

title: Emergency plans and drills for the main fire scenarios
plain: Do you know the fire plans for each fire scenario on this ship, and have you drilled them?
why: A fast, coordinated response is what stops a small tanker fire becoming a total loss.
checks: Fire plans for cargo deck, cargo tank, machinery space, pump room or compressor room, accommodation, store-room and galley
That each plan is specific to this ship
Fire drill records in the company format
Drill dates against the Bridge Log Book
Each fire plan drilled in the previous six months
ready: All fire plans, easy to find and ship-specific
Fire drill records for the last six months
Bridge Log Book for the last six months
Company emails for any deferred drill
traps: A fire plan is missing for one of the main scenarios
Plans are generic, not about this ship
Drill scenarios too easy or unrealistic
Drill date in the record does not match the Log Book
One fire scenario not drilled in six months
No fire drill within 24 hours of leaving port when more than 25% of crew had not done a fire drill on this ship in the previous month
say: We have a ship-specific plan for each main fire scenario, from deck to galley. Each one has been exercised in the last six months and recorded. If more than 25% of the crew have not done a fire drill on this ship in the previous month, we hold one within 24 hours of leaving port.

practice.q: Which fire scenarios do you have plans for?
a: Cargo deck, cargo tank, machinery space

practice.q: When must you drill after a crew change?
a: If more than 25% of crew have not done a drill on this ship in the previous month

practice.q: What do you do with equipment used in a drill?
a: Return it to full working condition at once
Fix any defects found as soon as possible

tip: Rotate the drill location and the scenario so that all seven fire plans are covered inside six months, and tick them off on one page.

title: Pollution drills under SOPEP or SMPEP
plain: Do you know the ship's oil or marine pollution plan, and have you drilled spill response?
why: A spill handled badly causes environmental damage, fines and port delays, so the crew must know their jobs.
checks: The SOPEP or SMPEP and that it is up to date
Plans for operational cargo and bunker spills
The contact list for this port, posted on the bridge or cargo control room
Spill drill records and Log Book dates
An officer interviewed about their duties in a spill
ready: SOPEP or SMPEP with current national contact points (electronic copy is fine if easy to find)
Port-specific contact list posted: DPA, port authority, P&I Club, agent, pollution reporting centre
Spill drill records covering cargo and bunker spills
Bridge Log Book for the last twelve months
Company emails for any deferred drill
traps: No SOPEP or SMPEP, or contact points out of date
No contact list prepared for the port of inspection
Drills do not cover both cargo and bunker spills
Officer unsure of their duties in a spill
Drill dates do not match the Log Book
Spill drill overdue
say: We carry the approved SOPEP and keep the contacts current. For every port we post a contact list on the bridge and in the cargo control room. We drill spills for both cargo and bunker operations and record each drill.

practice.q: Who is on your port contact list?
a: P&I Club and national pollution reporting centre
Extra contacts if trading in US waters

practice.q: What is your duty if there is a spill on deck?
a: Raise the alarm and stop the operation
Follow your role in the plan

practice.q: What spills do your drills cover?

tip: Make the port contact list part of the pre-arrival checklist so it is posted before the pilot boards.

title: Enclosed space rescue plan and drills
plain: Do you know the enclosed space rescue plan, and have you drilled it, including the hoisting gear?
why: Many enclosed space deaths are would-be rescuers, so a trained team and good rescue gear save lives.
checks: The enclosed space rescue plan for this ship
Drill records and attached entry permits where a real space was used
Rescue hoisting arrangements for cargo, ballast, bunker, void and cofferdam spaces
An officer or rating rigging and explaining the hoisting gear
Drill dates against the Log Book
ready: Enclosed space rescue plan, ship-specific
Drill records, with permit attached where a defined space was used
Rescue hoisting gear and loose equipment in good order
Bridge Log Book for the last twelve months
Company emails for any postponed drill
traps: No rescue plan, or it is generic
Drill record missing the entry permit when a real space was used
Rating or officer cannot rig or use the hoisting arrangement
Hoisting gear or loose equipment defective in any way
Drill unrealistic, or overdue
Dates do not match the Log Book
say: Our rescue plan is ship-specific. We drill at least every two months as SOLAS requires, covering PPE, communications, gas instruments, rescue gear and first aid. The attendant raises the alarm and never enters. Our people can rig the rescue hoist for each type of space.

practice.q: How often is the enclosed space drill?
a: At least once every two months
For crew with entry or rescue duties

practice.q: What must each drill include?
What does the attendant do if someone collapses?
a: Keep talking to the person and set up equipment outside

tip: Let different ratings rig the rescue hoist at each drill, so more than one person can do it on the day.

title: Security drills under the Ship Security Plan
plain: Do the Master and Ship Security Officer know the security drills the plan requires, and are they done on time?
why: Security drills test whether the crew can spot and respond to threats like intruders, piracy or stowaways.
checks: The schedule of security drills and exercises from the SSP
Records of completed drills in the company format
All scenarios required by the SSP done within the company time frame
Drill dates against the Log Book
Pre-entry drills with Ship Protection Measures if you entered a High Risk Area
ready: Security drill schedule
Drill and exercise records
Bridge Log Book for the last twelve months
Records of drills before entering a High Risk Area, with SPM in place
Company emails for any deferred drill
traps: No schedule of security drills
Master or SSO cannot explain the drills the SSP needs
Latest drill overdue
Required scenarios not all done in the set time
No SPM drill before entering a High Risk Area
Records not in the company format
say: We drill at least every three months, and within one week if more than 25% of the crew has changed. We cover scenarios like unauthorised visitors, restricted areas and mustering. The SSP is confidential, so I will show the schedule and records instead.

practice.q: How often do you hold security drills?
a: Within one week if more than 25% of crew changed

practice.q: What scenarios do you cover?
a: Recognising threat materials and restricted areas

practice.q: Before entering a High Risk Area, what do you do?
a: Drill with Ship Protection Measures in place
Test access points and lock down

tip: The inspector should not ask to see the SSP. Be ready to politely show only the front cover, and use the schedule and records to answer.

title: Lifeboat launching and abandon ship drills
plain: Do officers and ratings know how to launch the lifeboat, and are abandon ship drills done as required?
why: Lifeboat accidents often happen in drills because crews are not familiar with the equipment.
checks: The abandon ship procedure
The ship-specific lifeboat launching procedure for drills
Drill records, showing the lifeboat was exercised or launched as SOLAS requires
A rating explaining the launching procedure
Drill dates against the Log Book
ready: Abandon ship procedure
Ship-specific lifeboat launching procedure
Abandon ship drill records
Bridge Log Book for the last twelve months
Company emails for any postponed drill
traps: No abandon ship procedure or lifeboat launching procedure
Procedures too generic
Rating cannot explain the launching steps
Drill records not in the company format
Dates not matching the Log Book
Abandon ship drill overdue under company rules or SOLAS
say: Everyone on board does at least one abandon ship drill and one fire drill each month. We follow the maker's manual for the boat and our ship-specific procedure. Drills are run safely and at a safe speed, and we note lessons learnt for the next one.

practice.q: How often must crew do an abandon ship drill?
a: Within 24 hours of leaving port if over 25% of crew have not taken part in the previous month

practice.q: How do you keep lifeboat drills safe?
a: Check the boat and gear first
Risky parts, like lowering with full crew, only with special precautions

practice.q: What do you do if you find wear or corrosion?
a: Report it to the responsible officer at once

tip: Let ratings do the steps themselves during the drill while an officer watches, so each one can explain the launch in their own words.

title: Cargo vapour or liquid release plan and drills (gas carriers)
plain: Do you know the plan for a gas cargo leak or release, including fire, and have you drilled it?
why: A gas or liquid release can quickly turn into fire or brittle fracture, so the first minutes matter.
checks: Ship-specific plans for cargo vapour or liquid release, including fire
Plans cover containment leakage, connection rupture or spill, relief valve lifting and fire after leak
Drill records in the company format
Drill dates against the Log Book
Each scenario drilled within twelve months
ready: Emergency plans for cargo release, ship-specific
Drill records for the last twelve months
Bridge Log Book for the last twelve months
Precautions for any special recovery equipment, such as barrier punching devices
Cargo data sheets with spill, leak and fire actions
traps: No release plan on board
Plan too generic for this ship
Officer cannot explain the plan
Drill scenario unrealistic
A release scenario not drilled in twelve months
Latest drill overdue
say: Our plans cover containment leakage, connection rupture, relief valve lifting and fire after leakage. Each has been drilled within the year and recorded. The cargo data sheets tell us the spill, leak and firefighting actions for each product.

practice.q: Which release scenarios do your plans cover?
a: Connection rupture, pipeline fracture or spill

practice.q: What does the cargo data sheet tell you?

tip: Link each drill to a different scenario in your plan so all four are covered within the year.

title: Collision plan and drills
plain: Do you know the collision emergency plan, and have you drilled it on schedule?
why: After a collision, quick and organised action protects people, the environment and the ship.
checks: The ship-specific collision plan
Drill records in the company format
Drill dates against the Log Book
Whether the latest drill is within the company schedule
ready: Collision emergency plan
Collision drill records
Bridge Log Book for the last twelve months
ICS BPG checklist C4
Company emails for any postponed drill
traps: No collision plan
Plan not specific to this ship
Officer unfamiliar with the plan
Unrealistic drill scenario
Drill dates conflict with the Log Book
Drill overdue
say: Our collision plan covers what to do straight away, then the short and medium term, to protect people, the environment and the ship. We drill it on the company schedule and record it. Our bridge checklist is the first thing we pick up.

practice.q: What is your first priority after a collision?
a: Activate the plan and inform the company

practice.q: Who is in charge of the response?
a: The person named in the plan

tip: Run a table-top collision drill with the officers off watch; it costs nothing and shows who knows the plan.

title: Grounding plan and drills
plain: Do you know the grounding plan, including what data to collect and evidence to keep, and have you drilled it?
why: After grounding, the ship's strength and stability are unknown, so correct data and expert advice are vital.
checks: The ship-specific grounding plan
That the plan covers assessing the grounding and sending data to a technical adviser
That the plan covers saving ECDIS and VDR evidence
That the plan covers talking to the company and third parties
Drill records and Log Book dates
ready: Grounding emergency plan
Grounding drill records
Bridge Log Book for the last twelve months
ICS BPG checklist C5
Company emails for any postponed drill
traps: No grounding plan
Plan misses buoyancy, stability and strength assessment
Plan ignores saving ECDIS and VDR data
Plan has no communications with company or third parties
Unrealistic drill, or drill overdue
Dates not matching the Log Book
say: Our grounding plan tells us to collect data for a specialist adviser on buoyancy, stability and strength before deciding how to act. We save ECDIS and VDR data, and our plan sets out who we call. We drill it on schedule and record it.

practice.q: What does your grounding plan say about evidence?
Why do you need specialist advice?
a: You cannot know if the ship stays stable and intact while aground or refloating
The adviser predicts effects on the ship

tip: Know exactly how to save the VDR on your ship, and who does it; practise it in the drill.

title: Loss of propulsion plan and drills
plain: Do deck and engine officers know the loss of propulsion plan, and can a navigator estimate drift?
why: A drifting tanker with no engine can quickly end up on a lee shore, so both bridge and engine room must act fast.
checks: The ship-specific loss of propulsion plan
A navigation officer explaining how to estimate drift from wind, current and ship's head
An engineer officer knowing where the plan is and what it says
Drill records and Log Book dates
ready: Loss of propulsion plan
Drill records
Bridge Log Book for the last twelve months
ICS BPG checklist C1
Any previous drift records for the ship
traps: No plan for loss of propulsion
Plan too generic
Navigation officer cannot explain how to estimate drift
Engineer does not know where the plan is or what is in it
Unrealistic drill, or drill overdue
Dates not matching the Log Book
say: If we lose propulsion, we check how near hazards are and plot our drift on the chart using wind, current and our ship's head. Where possible we position the wind to improve drift. The engine room team follows the plan to restore power, and we drill it on schedule.

practice.q: How do you estimate drift of a disabled ship?
a: Plot rate and direction on a chart
Use wind, current and ship's head

practice.q: What can change drift if steering is lost?
a: Locking the rudder hard over to the downwind side

practice.q: Where is the plan kept?
a: Know where the plan is kept on board and what it says

tip: Engineers: know where the plan is. Navigators: practise a drift plot on the ECDIS during drills.

title: Electrical power failure plan and drills
plain: Do you know the blackout plan, and can officers explain recovery and estimate drift?
why: With no power the ship loses steering, pumps and cargo safety systems, so recovery must be quick and practised.
checks: The ship-specific plan for electrical power failure
Linked procedures: feeding back from the emergency switchboard and recovering after blackout
A navigation officer on estimating drift
An engineer officer on the plan and blackout recovery
Drill records and Log Book dates
ready: Power failure plan with engineering procedures it refers to
Drill records
Bridge Log Book for the last twelve months
ICS BPG checklist C3
Company emails for any postponed drill
traps: No plan for electrical power failure
Plan too generic
Navigator cannot estimate drift from wind, current and head
Engineer does not know location or content of the plan
Unrealistic drill, or drill overdue
Dates not matching the Log Book
say: Our plan covers blackout recovery and feeding the main board from the emergency switchboard. The engineers know the steps, and the bridge team knows how to estimate drift while we have no power. We drill it on schedule and record it.

practice.q: What procedures does your blackout plan refer to?
a: Feeding back from emergency to main switchboard

practice.q: How does the bridge team prepare for drift?
a: Plot drift using wind, current and ship's head

practice.q: What are your actions in a blackout?
a: Follow the plan steps to bring the situation under control
Recover power following the blackout procedure
Inform the bridge and watch for drift

tip: Make sure the drill date and time in the record match the Bridge Log Book entry.

title: Steering gear failure plan and drills
plain: Do you know the steering failure plan, and can an officer operate the emergency steering?
why: Loss of steering in confined water leads to grounding or collision, so emergency steering must work and be practised.
checks: The ship-specific steering gear failure plan
That the plan covers bridge control failure, single hydraulic or electrical failure and total failure
Drill records showing direct control testing from the steering gear compartment
An officer demonstrating emergency steering, communication and alternative power
A navigator explaining drift estimates
ready: Steering failure plan
Emergency steering drill records
Bridge Log Book for the last six months
Working emergency steering gear and communications
ICS BPG checklist C2
traps: Plan too generic for this ship
Officer cannot operate the emergency steering
Emergency steering gear defective
Drill did not include direct control
Navigator cannot estimate drift
Drill overdue or dates conflict with the Log Book
say: Emergency steering drills are done at least every three months, including direct control in the steering compartment, communication with the bridge and alternative power. I can demonstrate the operation if it is safe to do so.

practice.q: How often are emergency steering drills required?
a: At least once every three months

practice.q: What must the drill include?
a: Direct control in the steering gear compartment

practice.q: If steering is lost but the engine works, what can you do?
a: Lock the rudder in a fixed position
Use careful engine manoeuvres to control heading

practice.q: How do you operate the emergency steering?
a: Go to the steering gear room as the plan says
Steer to orders from the bridge on the agreed phone

tip: Practise the bridge to steering compartment call using the actual phone or radio. Many failures happen at that link.

title: Emergency towing plan and Emergency Towing Booklet
plain: Do officers know the Emergency Towing Booklet, where it is, and how to deploy the towing gear?
why: If the ship is disabled and drifting towards danger, a quick and correct tow connection can prevent a casualty.
checks: The ship-specific Emergency Towing Booklet (ETB)
Copies on the bridge, in a forecastle space and in the ship's office or cargo control room
Drill records and Log Book dates
A navigation and an engineer officer on where the ETB is and how towing gear is deployed
ready: Three copies of the ETB in the right places
Drill records for emergency towing
Bridge Log Book for the last twelve months
Towing equipment ready and known by crew
Company emails for any postponed drill
traps: No ETB on board
Copies missing from bridge, forecastle or office or CCR
Procedures not ship-specific
Officer does not know where the ETB is or how to deploy the gear
Unrealistic drill, or drill overdue
Dates not matching the Log Book
say: Our Emergency Towing Booklet is ship-specific, with rigging diagrams and safe working loads. There are copies on the bridge, in the forecastle and in the office. We drill towing and our officers know the deployment process.

practice.q: Where are your ETB copies kept?
a: In the ship's office or cargo control room

practice.q: What does the ETB contain?
a: Rigging diagrams, strong points and safe working loads
Communications plan for the towing ship

tip: Walk the forecastle with the ETB in hand and check each strong point and fitting actually matches the drawing.

title: Man overboard plan, rescue boat and drills
plain: Do you know the man overboard plan and how to launch and recover the rescue boat, and are drills done?
why: A person in the water has little time, and rescue boat accidents are a real danger if the crew is unfamiliar.
checks: The man overboard plan
The ship-specific procedure for launching and recovering the rescue boat in a drill
Drill records for man overboard and rescue boat launching
A navigation officer explaining the rescue boat procedure
A rating explaining their role on the muster list in a man overboard
ready: Man overboard emergency plan
Rescue boat launching and recovery procedure
Drill records, both man overboard and rescue boat (can be done separately)
Bridge Log Book for the last six months
Company emails for any postponed drill
traps: No man overboard plan or rescue boat procedure
Procedures too generic
Officer cannot explain launching and recovery
Rating does not know their muster list role
Unrealistic drill, or drill overdue under company rules or SOLAS
Dates not matching the Log Book
say: Our man overboard plan and rescue boat procedure are ship-specific. The rescue boat is launched with its crew and manoeuvred in the water at least every three months, and monthly where reasonable. If we launch with headway, we do so in sheltered waters under an experienced officer.

practice.q: How often must the rescue boat be launched?
a: Monthly as far as reasonable and practicable
At least once every three months in all cases

practice.q: What is your role in a man overboard?
When can you launch while the ship has headway?

tip: Ratings are asked about the muster list, so have each person read their own line aloud during briefings.

title: Recovery of persons from the water
plain: Do you know your plan for getting a person out of the water, and have you drilled it?
why: Getting someone aboard is often harder than finding them, and the rescuers can be hurt without a plan.
checks: The ship-specific plan for recovery of persons from the water
Drill records in the company format
Drill dates against the Log Book
A rating explaining the plan and their role
ready: Recovery from the water plan, naming the equipment to use
Drill records (can be combined with man overboard drills)
Bridge Log Book for the last twelve months
Company emails for any deferred drill
traps: No plan for recovery from the water, or too generic
Rating does not know their role
Officer cannot explain the plan
Drill scenario unrealistic
Records not in the company format, or dates not matching the Log Book
Drill overdue
say: Our plan names the equipment we will use and the limits for a safe recovery, such as freeboard, weather, waves and manoeuvrability. We drill it with man overboard drills, record it, and every rating knows their job.

practice.q: What conditions does your plan consider?
a: Manoeuvrability and freeboard of the ship
Where casualties can be brought aboard
Wind, waves, swell and safety of navigation

practice.q: What is your part in a recovery?
a: Describe the equipment you would use

tip: Add a recovery step to your normal man overboard drill so the crew practise both parts together.

title: Flooding plans and drills

Drill records in the company format
Drill dates against the Log Book
Each flooding plan drilled in the last twelve months
ready: All flooding plans, ship-specific
Flooding drill records for the last twelve months
Bridge Log Book for the last twelve months
ICS BPG checklist C8
Company emails for any deferred drill
traps: A flooding plan is missing
Plans are not ship-specific
Officer unfamiliar with the plans
Unrealistic drill scenario
One flooding scenario not drilled in twelve months
Records not in the company format, or dates not matching the Log Book
say: We have plans for machinery space, pump room, forecastle and hull breach flooding. Each has been drilled in the last year. Machinery space flooding is the most urgent because we could lose power, pumps and buoyancy.

practice.q: Which flooding scenarios do you have plans for?
Why is machinery space flooding so serious?
a: Loss of bilge and fire pumps

tip: Plan the drill schedule so every flooding scenario is drilled within twelve months.

title: LNG bunkering emergency plans and drills

Drill records in the company format
Whether all required scenarios were done on time

Emergency plans if not inside the manual
LNG bunkering drill records
Bridge Log Book for the last twelve months
Details of any unusual actions, such as couplings that open and close the opposite way
traps: No fuel handling manual for LNG bunkers

Procedures not ship-specific
Officer unfamiliar with the emergency procedures
Drill scenarios not completed in the company time frame
Drill overdue, or records not in the company format

practice.q: What situations does an LNG bunkering emergency plan cover?

practice.q: What hazards are special to LNG?

title: Cargo leak into double hull spaces

Equipment on deck: stowage, availability and condition
Whether the officer knows where the equipment is
Records of electrical continuity tests for inerting hoses

practice.q: What options do you have to keep the hull tank atmosphere safe?

P/V valves or vent valves with flame screens

practice.q: What do you check on inerting hoses?

title: Emergency fire pump
plain: Can crew start the emergency fire pump, and is it tested and its location kept clear?

checks: Company procedure and ship-specific starting instructions posted beside the pump
Access to the pump space: airlock doors closed, second access not locked
Inlet and outlet valves marked and open
Witness a start and see required pressure through anchor washes or another outlet
Diesel engine fuel level and quick closing valve, and test records
ready: Clear starting instructions in the ship's working language beside the pump
Maintenance and test records, including diesel engine and fuel quick closing valve
Enough fuel in the tank for 3 hours, plus 15 hours more available outside the space
Marked fuel closing devices
Sub-zero fuel if trading in cold areas
traps: No company procedure, or no posted starting instructions
Airlock door held open, or second door locked
Engine does not start within three attempts
Pump does not reach pressure or flow without extra manual steps
Leaks, defects or closed valves where pump is remote
Less than 3 hours fuel in tank, or under 18 hours total
Records missing
say: Starting instructions are posted at the pump for anyone who might need them. We test it regularly and keep records, including the quick closing valve. The access doors stay closed and the second access is never locked. Fuel is kept for the required running time.

practice.q: How do you start the emergency fire pump?
a: Check fuel and valves are set
Know the manual starting method too

practice.q: What fuel must be available?
a: Enough in the tank for 3 hours

practice.q: What do you check at the pump space?
a: Airlock doors closed and not held open
Suction and discharge valves open and marked

tip: Let a deck rating start the pump with instructions at the next test. The source says the posted steps are for non-engineers.

title: Fire dampers and ventilation stops
plain: Do you know where the fire dampers, ventilation closing devices and remote fan stops are, and do they work?
why: Shutting off air and fans from outside a space is how you starve a fire and stop it spreading.
checks: List of closing devices for ventilation inlets and outlets and their required position during cargo operations
A sample of closing devices: free to operate, marked with the space served and open/shut
Remote fan stops for accommodation and machinery spaces, clearly identified
Maintenance plan and test records for dampers, skylights and fan stops
An officer and a rating explaining location, purpose and operation
ready: Ship-specific list of closing devices with required port and cargo-operation status
Dampers, skylights and closing devices free, sealed and clear of obstruction
Markings for space served, open/shut, warning notices (for example battery lockers) and cargo-time position
Maintenance plan including dampers, skylights, closing devices and fan stops
Test records for fire dampers: quarterly local and annual remote tests
traps: Crew do not know location, purpose or operation
Closing devices seized or ineffective: corroded, worn gaskets, seized dogs
Missing marks for space, open/shut, warning notice or cargo-time position
Access to closing devices or fan stops blocked
Remote closing devices stopped from closing fully by obstructions
Maintenance plan missing these items, or records incomplete or not matching reality
say: We keep a list of every ventilation closing device and its required position during cargo operations. Each is marked with its space and open or shut position. Fire dampers are tested locally every quarter and remotely every year, and records are kept.

practice.q: How do you stop the fans for the accommodation or machinery space?
a: Use the remote stops, outside the space
Machinery space fans have separate stops from other spaces

practice.q: What position should a ventilation closing device be in during cargo operations?
How often are fire dampers tested?

tip: Walk the deck with the list during routine checks: if a damper cannot move freely by hand, it will not close in a fire.

title: Fixed fire detection and alarm system
plain: Do officers know the fire detection and alarm system, and is it working, tested and maintained?
why: Early detection and a clear alarm give people time to escape and fight the fire.
checks: Company procedure for operation, testing and maintenance
Central panel: system working, no faults, zone information displayed, all zones and detectors active
Test and calibration records, and the Engine Room Logbook
Correct test equipment for each type of detector
Any delay programmed into the alarm, and whether machinery spaces were unattended with a zone isolated or defective
ready: Company procedure and manufacturer's manual
Weekly, monthly and annual test records, including detector tests and output signal tests
Test equipment suited to each detector type
Information next to each panel about spaces and sections
Emergency power supply check records
Spare parts and instructions for testing
traps: No company procedure for the system
Panel showing a fault, or system not working
A detector covered or disabled
Machinery space unattended while a zone was isolated or the system was defective
Delay between detection and alarm where panel space is not manned
No suitable detector test equipment, or no zone information at panel
Records incomplete, or actions in plan not actually done
say: The system is fully active with no faults. Detectors are tested at the set frequency using the right equipment for each type. If a zone must be isolated for work, it is documented and the machinery space is not run unattended. I know of any programmed alarm delay.

practice.q: What would you do if the system shows a fault?
a: Do not run the machinery space unattended while defective
Use alternative arrangements such as patrols

practice.q: How are different detectors tested?
a: Using the proper test device for each type
At the frequency in the company procedure

practice.q: What does the alarm system test include?
a: Output signals to other fire safety systems

tip: Keep a spare set of the right test devices and a zone list at the panel, not only in the office.

title: Machinery space fixed CO2 system
plain: Do officers know the CO2 system and how to release it, and are instructions posted and the system ready?
why: CO2 is the last defence for a machinery space fire, and it is also deadly to anyone who enters the space unsafely.
checks: Safe entry instructions posted at each entrance to the CO2 room
Release station: procedure, instructions and warning notices posted
CO2 bottle room and cabinets, with keys provided if locked
Inspection and service data and maintenance plan records
An officer explaining purpose and operation, including whether the pins should be in or out
ready: Safe entry notice: start ventilation, wait a set time, use gas monitor, notify entry and exit
Release instructions and warnings at control stations
Break-glass key box next to locked doors
Maintenance plan including the CO2 system: monthly, annual, survey-time work
No blanked branch pipes, inhibited nozzles or levers
traps: No safe entry procedure posted at the CO2 room entrance
Officer does not know the entry precautions or system operation
Room or cabinets locked with no keys
Release procedure and warnings not posted at the release station
Maintenance plan missing the system, or records incomplete or not real
System defective, or not ready for immediate use
say: Safe entry rules are at each entrance: ventilate, wait, use a personal gas monitor and report entry and exit. The release steps are displayed at the release station. I know the pins are either in or out depending on the manufacturer's instructions.

practice.q: How do you release the CO2?
a: Make sure the space is evacuated and sealed
Pre-release alarm gives people time to leave

practice.q: How do you enter the CO2 room safely?
a: Tell someone on entry and exit

practice.q: Are the pins in or out when the system is ready?

tip: The inspector will ask whether the pins stay in or out. Know the answer for your system from the maker's manual.

title: Machinery space high-expansion foam system
plain: Do officers know the high-expansion foam system, and is it ready with foam in date and instructions posted?
why: If the foam is out of date, wrong for the cargo or the controls are unclear, the system may fail when needed.
checks: Operating instructions in the ship's working language posted near the control station
Valves clearly identified with standby and operating status
Foam concentrate annual test certificate showing it is fit for use, and foam tank at the right level
Foam compatible with the cargo if it also protects the pump room
Maintenance records, including five-yearly proportioner tests
ready: Posted instructions and warnings at the release station
Foam test certificates: first test within 3 years of manufacture, then yearly
Protein-based alcohol-resistant foam stability test before delivery and each year
System manual showing foam quantity needed
Maintenance plan: monthly, quarterly, annual and five-year tasks
Breathing apparatus rule for re-entry after discharge
traps: Release instructions not posted in the working language
Valves not identified, or required position not shown
Foam concentrate test overdue, or certificate says unfit
Foam not compatible with the cargo carried for a pump room system
Foam proportioners not tested at five-year service
Plan incomplete, records missing or not true, or system defective
say: Operating instructions are posted in our working language and the valves are marked with standby and operating status. Foam concentrate is tested annually and the certificate is on file. Anyone re-entering after a discharge wears breathing apparatus.

practice.q: How often is the foam tested?
a: First test not more than 3 years after manufacture

practice.q: Why wear breathing apparatus after discharge?
a: Products of combustion in the foam blanket

practice.q: What if the system also covers the pump room?
a: Foam must suit the cargoes carried

tip: Photograph the foam tank level gauge and test certificate dates and keep them with the maintenance record.

title: Machinery space water-spray or water mist system
plain: Do officers know the fixed water-spray or water mist system, and is it ready with correct pressure and posted instructions?
why: These systems cool and smother machinery space fires, and poor water quality or wrong valve settings can stop them working.
checks: Operating instructions in the ship's working language posted at control stations
Valves clearly identified, standby and operating status shown
System at the correct pressure with inlet and outlet valves correctly set
Maintenance records including quarterly water quality checks
An officer explaining the purpose and operation
ready: Posted release procedure and warning notices
Weekly, monthly, annual, five-year and ten-year maintenance records
Ten-year servicing including hydrostatic test and internal examination of pressure cylinders
Quarterly water quality records meeting the maker's guidelines
Maintenance plan that includes the system
traps: Instructions not posted in the working language
Valves or controls not marked with purpose and required status
No quarterly water quality records, or records outside the maker's limits
Maintenance plan missing the system, or incomplete
Officer unfamiliar with the system
System defective, or records do not match what was done
say: Instructions are posted at the release stations in our working language and valves are marked. We keep the system at the correct pressure and check water quality every quarter against the maker's guidance. The plan covers weekly to ten-yearly tasks.

practice.q: How do you operate the system?
a: Check valves are set as required
Know where release controls are, outside the space

practice.q: What water checks are required?

tip: Put the quarterly water quality check on the PMS as its own job so it is not lost inside a larger task.

title: Fire pumps, fire main, isolating valves and hydrants
plain: Do officers know the fire pumps, fire main, isolating valves and hydrants, and do they all work?
why: Water on deck and in the machinery space is the first firefighting tool, so any weak pipe or stuck valve is a risk.
checks: Remote start of a fire pump from the bridge or fire control station, with pressure held at an outlet
Deck fire main, especially underneath, for corrosion, patching or rope wear
Pump suction and delivery valves open
Hydrants and isolating valves moved by hand to see they work freely
Officer explaining pump start, isolating valves and the drain point
ready: Pressure indication on the bridge or fire control station
Isolating valves and hydrants clearly marked and moving freely
Fire main in good condition, no hard rust or temporary repairs
Plan for sub-zero conditions so the system stays ready
Maintenance records: monthly, quarterly and annual checks
traps: Fire pump cannot be started remotely from the bridge or fire control station
No way to read fire main pressure on the bridge or at the fire control station
Hydrant or isolating valves stiff, closed or unmarked
Hard rust, patches or temporary repairs on fire main
Pump suction or delivery valve closed
Officer cannot explain pump start, isolation valves or drain point
Records incomplete or not matching actual condition
say: We can start a fire pump from the bridge and see the pressure at the outlet. Isolating valves and hydrants move freely and are marked. I know where the deck fire main drain is, and our plan covers sub-zero conditions.

practice.q: How do you start a fire pump remotely?
a: From the bridge or fire control station
Check it reaches and keeps pressure

practice.q: Where are isolating valves fitted on a tanker?
a: On the tank deck at intervals not more than 40 m
At the poop front in a protected position

practice.q: What is the drain point for?

tip: On deck rounds, try a hydrant and an isolating valve and note the location, so over time you cover the whole system.

title: Galley fire systems and fire prevention
plain: Do galley staff know the fire extinguishing equipment, and are ranges, vents and filters free of grease?
why: Most galley fires start from grease build-up, and galley staff are the first people on scene.
checks: Galley ranges, grease traps, flue pipes and vent filter cowls free of fat
Fixed system for deep fat fryers: serviced, nozzles clean, blow-out caps fitted if needed
Fire dampers and fan stop points marked and free to operate
Portable extinguishers and fire blankets stowed and not blocked
Fire doors and serving hatch shutters free to close, detectors not disabled
A galley crew member explaining the extinguishing system, portable equipment or ventilation stops
ready: Posted instructions for the galley fixed extinguishing system
Procedure for inspection and cleaning of ranges, flues and filters, with records
Maintenance plan including galley systems, dampers and fan stops
Fixed system service records
Rule that no deep fat frying is done without a fixed extinguishing system
traps: No posted instructions for the fixed system
Galley staff cannot explain the equipment
Grease on ranges, traps, flues, nozzles, detector heads or filter cowls
Deep fat frying in open pans or a fryer with no fixed system
Fire doors or serving hatch shutters held open
Extinguishers blocked or missing
Plan or records incomplete, or fixed system defective
say: The galley is cleaned on a schedule, including the filters and flues. The fryer has a fixed extinguishing system with posted instructions, and I know how it works. Extinguishers and the fire blanket are in place, and no flames are used in port at a petroleum berth.

practice.q: What do you do if the fryer catches fire?
a: Use the fixed system as posted
Shut off power and stop the fans

practice.q: How do you stop galley ventilation?
a: Use the fan stop point in or near the galley

practice.q: What cleaning must be done?

tip: Ask the cook to show the inspector the fryer system release. Galley staff who can explain it simply make a strong impression.

title: Deck water-spray system (gas carriers)
plain: Do officers know the deck water-spray system for cooling and crew protection, and is it clear, tested and maintained?
why: The water spray keeps tanks, manifolds and accommodation cool in a cargo area fire, and clogged nozzles or corroded pipes can stop it.
checks: Remote controls, with operating instructions posted and valves marked and set
Piping, especially underneath, for corrosion or patching
A sample of nozzles for clogging
Isolating and stop valves moved by hand
Officer explaining pump start, isolating valves and the deck drain point
ready: Posted instructions at the control station, with access clear
Maintenance plan including the water-spray system
Records of weekly, monthly, annual and five-year tasks
Records of removing orifice plates and end caps and flushing debris
Cleaning of in-line filters, fresh water flushing and drying
traps: Officer unfamiliar with location, purpose or operation
Instructions not posted, or access to controls blocked
Valves or controls not marked or set properly
Stop or isolating valves stiff or unmarked
Clogged nozzles
Hard rust or temporary repairs on pipework
No proof that orifice plates and end caps were removed and the system flushed
Plan or records incomplete or not true
say: The water-spray controls are clear with posted instructions. We test it and flush the pipework, removing orifice plates and end caps to clear scale. I know how to start the pumps and where the isolating valves and drain points are.

practice.q: What does the system protect?
a: Cargo tank domes and exposed parts
Accommodation and bridge boundaries facing cargo area
Lifeboats, liferafts and muster stations facing the cargo area

practice.q: What maintenance do you do?
a: Remove orifice plates and end caps and flush debris
Flush with fresh water and dry

tip: After each fresh water flush, drain and dry the pipework and note it in the PMS so the inspector sees it was done.

title: Fixed fire system in cargo handling spaces (gas carriers)
plain: Do officers know the fixed fire system in the compressor or cargo machinery rooms, and is it ready with notices posted?
why: This system protects enclosed cargo machinery spaces, and the gas is dangerous if anyone is still inside or enters unsafely.
checks: Company procedure with description, operating instructions and maintenance plan
Bottle space safe entry notice at each entrance
Notice at each protected room entrance saying a fixed system protects it
Release station: instructions and warnings posted, keys available if locked
Maintenance and inspection records, and officer's knowledge, including pins in or out
ready: Procedure for operation, inspection and maintenance (may be in the cargo manual)
Entry instructions: start fan, wait, personal gas monitor, tell the OOW on entry and exit
Break-glass key box at locked doors
Notice at CO2 controls: for firefighting only, not inerting, due to static risk
Records of maintenance
Nothing blanked or inhibited
traps: No company procedure with description, instructions and plan
No safe entry procedure posted at bottle space doors
Room entrances not marked as protected by a fixed system
Doors locked with no keys
Instructions and warnings not posted at the release station
System not ready: blanked pipes, inhibited nozzles or levers
Officer unfamiliar with operation or entry precautions
Records incomplete, or system defective
say: The entrances to our compressor and motor rooms are marked as protected by a fixed system. Release instructions and warnings are posted. Before entering the bottle space we ventilate, wait, carry a gas monitor and tell the OOW. CO2 is used only for firefighting, never for inerting.

practice.q: What must you do before entering the bottle space?
a: Notify the OOW of entry and exit

practice.q: Why can CO2 not be used for inerting?
a: A notice at the controls says this

practice.q: What is a key concern before release?
a: Everyone must evacuate the space first
The system is single shot, so be sure there is fire

tip: Know whether your system uses CO2 or a clean agent. The source says either is possible.

title: Fixed dry chemical powder system (gas carriers)
plain: Do officers know the deck dry powder system, and is it ready with instructions posted and checks done?
why: Dry powder is the main tool against gas fires at manifolds and on deck, and caked or wet powder will not work.
checks: System components and controls in the cargo area
Operating instructions posted near controls, in the working language
Valves and controls marked as in the instructions
Inspection and servicing data at control stations
Records for annual nitrogen agitation and two-yearly moisture test
Officer explaining purpose and operation
ready: Instructions at each operating station
Monthly pressure gauge checks in range
Annual agitation of the powder
Two-yearly moisture test of a powder sample
Ten-yearly hydrostatic or non-destructive test of powder containers
Maintenance plan including the system
traps: Instructions not posted in the working language at each station
Controls and valves not marked as per instructions
Officer unfamiliar with the system or the maintenance plan
Annual agitation or two-yearly moisture test records missing
Plan missing the system or required checks
Records not matching what was really done, or system defective
say: Operating instructions are at every station in our working language and valves are marked. We check pressure monthly, agitate the powder with nitrogen yearly and test a sample for moisture every two years. I can explain how to operate it.

practice.q: How do you use the system?
a: Monitors and hand hoses can be used

practice.q: What periodic checks are needed?

tip: Put the yearly agitation and two-yearly moisture sample into the PMS so they cannot be missed.

title: Paint locker fixed fire system
plain: Do officers know the fixed fire system in the paint locker and other flammable liquid lockers, and is paint stored safely?
why: Paint and thinners burn fiercely, so the locker system and safe storage keep a small fire from becoming a big one.
checks: Release instructions posted outside the locker
Ventilation fan controls and closing devices marked
Where a portable extinguisher is used instead, the inlet port is marked
CO2 system: warning sign against using it for inerting
Seawater spray system: nozzles free of salt, stores not stacked above nozzle height
ready: Company procedure for paint and flammable liquid storage, including where to store extra paint during maintenance
Paints kept only in closed containers
Maintenance plan covering the locker system, with records
Clear access to the system controls
Cargo sample lockers in the cargo area are not covered by the same SOLAS requirement
traps: No instructions posted outside the locker
Officer unfamiliar with the system
Paint or flammables stored in a place not made for them
Paint in open containers
Tins stacked above the water spray nozzles
Access to controls blocked
Plan or records incomplete, or system defective
say: Paints are stored only in closed containers in the paint locker. Release instructions are posted outside, and the controls are clear. We keep stock below the spray nozzle level and check the nozzles for salt build-up.

practice.q: How do you release the system?
a: Follow the instructions posted outside the space

practice.q: What storage rules apply?
a: Designated lockers, with a company plan for overflow stores

practice.q: What must not be done with a CO2 system?
a: Do not use CO2 to inert the space (static ignition hazard)

tip: During a riding-team maintenance period, plan paint storage in advance so stock never ends up outside the locker.

title: Machinery space local application fire-fighting system
plain: Do officers know the local water-based fire system in the engine room, and is it ready in the right mode?
why: This system fights a fire at the source without stopping the engine, so it must be armed correctly, especially when the engine room is unattended.
checks: Company procedure on when to set automatic release mode, including unattended operation
Instructions posted at control stations in the ship's working language
Water supply valves and manual branch valves open and marked or colour coded
Dedicated tank has a low-level alarm or marked minimum level
Control panel powered and set to automatic or remote, local release stations marked, detectors active
ready: Procedure for automatic and manual release modes
Posted operating instructions
Valve and zone marking
Remote panels in the wheelhouse powered on
Maintenance records for weekly to ten-yearly checks
Plan including the system
traps: No company procedure on automatic release mode
Officer unsure of the required mode or operation
Instructions not posted in the working language
System in manual mode while the machinery space is unattended
Supply or branch valves closed
Tank low-level alarm missing or minimum level not marked
Detectors deactivated
Records incomplete, or system defective
say: Our procedure says when the system must be in automatic mode, always when the engine room is unattended. Instructions are posted, valves are open and marked, and the tank level is monitored. I know the release mode for both attended and unattended operation.

practice.q: What mode must the system be in when the engine room is unattended?
a: The mode set by company procedure
Manual-only release is not acceptable when unattended

practice.q: What do you check at the system?
a: Water supply and branch valves open
Tank level alarm or marked level
Control panel powered and set correctly

tip: Add the release mode to the UMS handover checklist so it is checked every time the engine room goes unattended.

title: Pump temperature sensors in the pump room
plain: Do officers know why pump temperature sensors are fitted, and are alarms set, tested and records kept?
why: A hot bearing or seal in a pump room can ignite cargo vapour, so early warning and correct alarm settings prevent fire.
checks: Company procedure for operating, checking and testing the temperature sensing system
The monitoring panel: working, no faults, similar pumps showing similar readings, alarm settings displayed
Records of temperatures for pumps in operation
A demonstration of one alarm set point if safe
In the pump room: sensors connected, no temporary cooling, no mechanical seal leaks
ready: Company procedure covering recording, alarm actions, accuracy checks and set points
Readings records for bulkhead glands, bearings and casings of cargo, ballast and stripping pumps
Maker's manual and test records
Alarm set points confirmed, within company limit
Record of who can change alarm set points, and when
Audible and visual alarm test records
traps: No company procedure
Officer does not know the alarm settings or what to do on a high temperature alarm
No temperature records for pumps in operation
Sensors not checked or alarms not tested at the set frequency
Sensor out of service or disconnected
Alarm set higher than company limit allows
Temporary cooling on pump bearings
Seal leaking liquid or mist
say: We record temperatures of glands, bearings and casings while pumps run. Alarm settings are displayed and within our company limit. We check sensor accuracy and test the alarms at the set frequency. A high temperature alarm means we stop the pump and investigate.

practice.q: What do you do on a high temperature alarm?
Where are sensors fitted?
Which pumps are covered?
a: Ballast pumps, stripping pumps and tank cleaning pumps (in the pump room, driven through bulkheads)

tip: If the panel is only in the engine room, make sure the cargo watch officer knows the alarm indication in the CCR and records readings. Applies to ships with a pump room only.

title: Deck foam system and portable applicators
plain: Do officers and ratings know how to use the deck foam system, monitors and applicators, and is it ready?
why: Deck foam is the main weapon against spill fires and tank fires, and wrong connections or bad foam waste the first minutes.
checks: Instructions in the working language posted at the foam room and control station
Valves identified with standby and operating status
Annual foam test certificate showing foam fit for use, foam tank at the right level
Foam compatible with the cargo carried
Isolating valves and monitors moved through their full range
A rating explaining use of foam monitors and applicators
ready: Foam concentrate certificates: first test not more than 3 years after manufacture, then yearly
Stability test for protein-based alcohol-resistant foam before delivery and yearly
Five-yearly proportioner test records
System manual showing foam quantity needed
Foam applicators set up on the foam main, not the fire main
Maintenance plan with monthly, quarterly, annual and five-year tasks
traps: Instructions not posted in the working language
Valves or controls not clearly identified
Foam tank not at required level
Foam test overdue or certificate says unfit
Foam incompatible with the cargo and no approved alternative
Proportioners not tested at five-yearly service
Officer or rating cannot explain the foam system or use
Monitors or valves stiff, applicators connected to the fire main
Plan or records incomplete, or system defective
say: Instructions are posted at the foam room and valves are marked. Our foam is tested yearly and is compatible with our cargoes. We can use it to fight spill fires, stop ignition of spilt oil and fight fires in a ruptured tank, and our ratings know the monitors and applicators.

practice.q: What is the deck foam system for?
a: Stopping ignition of spilt oil not yet burning

practice.q: What mistake with portable applicators is common?
a: Connecting to the fire main instead of the foam main

practice.q: How often is foam concentrate tested?
a: First test within 3 years of manufacture

tip: Let a rating set up an applicator at the manifold during a drill and check which main it is connected to.
